Issue #97: [Format contract] Define parity and omissions for Markdown, LaTeX and DOCX/OOXML

## Problem

SourceRight's public `citations` usage advertises `<manuscript.txt|manuscript.docx>`, while the implementation reads any non-DOCX input as UTF-8 text. Markdown therefore works but is undocumented and its syntax can be mistaken for content. LaTeX works through citation-macro recognition but is likewise absent from the file-format contract. DOCX support reads only `word/document.xml`, so genuine OOXML footnotes/endnotes and other story parts are not part of direct reconciliation.

This is a format-contract and coverage gap, not a claim that existing work in #13 and #20-#22 failed. Current targeted LaTeX and main-document DOCX tests pass.

## Evidence and diagnostics

- `read_manuscript_text` special-cases `.docx`; every other extension goes through `read_to_string`.
- DOCX extraction opens only `word/document.xml`.
- the intake model recognizes Markdown headings and text labelled `footnotes`/`endnotes`, but direct OOXML story-part extraction is separate and absent.
- one real Markdown/DOCX pair produced identical totals: 33 occurrences, 2 matches and 57 issues against the same test workspace.
- Markdown comments/headings and note text can enter downstream heuristics because no syntax-aware masking contract is advertised.

## What was tried

- tested the same manuscript as `.md` and `.docx`;
- reran LaTeX reconciliation tests and DOCX superscript-normalization test;
- inspected OOXML package reading and current documentation.

## Options and tradeoffs

1. **Recommended: publish a support matrix plus normalized intermediate representation.** Define supported constructs and losses for `.txt`, `.md`, `.tex` and `.docx`; normalize body, callouts, notes, references and provenance spans before reconciliation. More design work, but it gives cross-format parity a testable meaning.
2. **Extend the current direct readers incrementally.** Add Markdown masking, explicit `.tex` docs and `footnotes.xml`/`endnotes.xml` relationship traversal. Faster, but risks format-specific behavior drifting apart.
3. **Require external conversion to a canonical text/AST format.** Smaller SourceRight surface, but pushes provenance and conversion quality onto users.

## OOXML-specific considerations

- traverse package relationships rather than assuming fixed story-part names;
- distinguish note callouts from note bodies;
- preserve part/paragraph/run provenance;
- define behavior for tracked changes, deleted text, fields, hyperlinks, tables, headers and comments;
- fail or warn explicitly for unsupported/encrypted/corrupt packages.

## Contingency and fallback

- If full OOXML coverage is deferred, detect footnote/endnote relationships and emit a prominent `docx.story_parts_omitted` diagnostic.
- Recommend audited export to plain text/Markdown, retaining source and export hashes.
- Keep raw Markdown/LaTeX acceptance, but label it text-mode unless syntax-aware handling was applied.

## Acceptance criteria

- CLI help and docs accurately name supported extensions and constructs.
- fixtures cover equivalent citations in text, Markdown, LaTeX and DOCX body/footnote/endnote forms.
- reports identify the source format, normalization path and omitted constructs.
- cross-format tests compare citation identities and provenance, not only counts.
- unsupported content produces explicit diagnostics rather than silent omission.

Issue #1481: Two wiki pages say selecting a location shows everything nested beneath it; the filter is direct-only, so a parent reads as empty

## What happens

Two wiki pages tell the reader that selecting a location shows what is nested inside it as well as what is directly in it. It does not — the filter is a flat match on the item's own location, so a parent that holds nothing of its own reads "0 items match" even when its children are full.

`Core-Concepts.md:33-34`:

> Selecting a location filters the inventory to just what's in it (**and everything nested beneath it**).

`Locations-and-Stock.md:29-30`:

> Selecting a location **filters** the inventory to what it holds, including everything nested beneath it.

Both pages contradict themselves elsewhere. `Locations-and-Stock.md:48` has a whole section called "Drilling into a sub-location", which exists precisely because a parent with no items of its own would otherwise dead-end; `:314` says "Only items placed **directly** in a location count toward its space used"; and `:402` documents a *This location / With sub-locations* switch on the Statistics tab, which would be pointless if the list rolled up by default.

## Where

- [docs/wiki/Core-Concepts.md:33-34](https://github.com/BootBlock/Gubbins/blob/48554edeaf159eda390352e805fc7eaea74a2184/docs/wiki/Core-Concepts.md#L33-L34)
- [docs/wiki/Locations-and-Stock.md:29-30](https://github.com/BootBlock/Gubbins/blob/48554edeaf159eda390352e805fc7eaea74a2184/docs/wiki/Locations-and-Stock.md#L29-L30)
- [src/db/repositories/item/core.ts:936-939](https://github.com/BootBlock/Gubbins/blob/48554edeaf159eda390352e805fc7eaea74a2184/src/db/repositories/item/core.ts#L936-L939) — `buildListFilter`, shared by `list` and `count`, pushes `location_id = ?` and nothing else
- [src/features/inventory/InventoryScreen.tsx:443](https://github.com/BootBlock/Gubbins/blob/48554edeaf159eda390352e805fc7eaea74a2184/src/features/inventory/InventoryScreen.tsx#L443) — passes the selected id straight through
- [src/features/inventory/components/SubLocationNav.tsx](https://github.com/BootBlock/Gubbins/blob/48554edeaf159eda390352e805fc7eaea74a2184/src/features/inventory/components/SubLocationNav.tsx) — the drill-down that exists because the filter is direct-only

## How to reproduce / how it was verified

In a browser: create a parent location, nest a child under it, and put an item in the child only. Select the parent.

Observed: the header reads `Items 0 · Sub-locations 1`, the result line reads `0 items match`, and the list shows "No items here — open a location to see what's inside."

Expected per both wiki pages: the child's item is listed.

The repository confirms it directly — `count({ locationId: parent })` returns `0` while `count({ locationId: child })` returns `1`.

There is no descendant expansion anywhere in the item-list path: no recursive CTE, no `includeDescendants` flag. The only `WITH RECURSIVE` in `LocationRepository.ts` (`:202`, `:951`) walks *ancestors*, for cycle prevention.

A second-order slip rides along with it. ## Expected

Either the pages say the filter is direct-only and point at the sub-location drill-down, or the filter rolls up. The rest of both pages, and the Statistics tab's own *This location / With sub-locations* switch, are written on the assumption that it is direct-only.

## Impact

Severity: wrong-data

Anyone with a nested location tree, on the two pages that teach the mental model. A user who reads either sentence and sees an empty parent will conclude their items are lost or their stock has moved, when neither is true. `Core-Concepts.md` is linked from Home as the page that explains "the handful of ideas", so it is close to the first thing a new reader is told.

## Suggested direction

A copy fix on both pages is the smaller change, and matches what every other paragraph on them already assumes. Worth deciding as one edit, since the two sentences say the same thing.

Issue #10755: [Bug] ConsumeQueue truncation leaves orphaned ConsumeQueueExt entries

## RocketMQ version

`develop` at `a06836dd564e5e43115493f775626cf98d51d10e`

## Describe the bug

`ConsumeQueue.truncateDirtyLogicFiles` updates the ConsumeQueue positions but skips truncating the associated `ConsumeQueueExt` during every normal partial-truncation path.

The method tracks the last retained extension address in `maxExtAddr`, and its tail calls:

```java
consumeQueueExt.truncateByMaxAddress(maxExtAddr);
```

However, scanning returns directly when it reaches the first dirty CQ entry, the end of a full valid CQ file, or an unwritten slot. Those returns bypass the extension truncation. The tail is only reached after all CQ files have been deleted or no CQ file exists; in that case `maxExtAddr` remains `1`, which is not an extension address, so `truncateByMaxAddress` is a no-op.

## Deterministic reproduction

1. Create a file-backed `ConsumeQueue` with `enableConsumeQueueExt=true`.
2. Write four CQ entries with physical offsets `0`, `100`, `200`, and `300`, using distinct tag codes so that four CQExt units are created.
3. Record the raw extension addresses stored by CQ entries 2 and 3.
4. Call `truncateDirtyLogicFiles(200)`, retaining entries 0 and 1.
5. Write replacement entries at CQ offsets 2 and 3 with different tag codes.
6. Flush, load a second `ConsumeQueue` from the same directory, and call `recover()`.
7. Read the extension unit at the original address of entry 2.

Expected:

- CQExt is truncated together with CQ.
- Replacement entries reuse the truncated extension addresses.
- After reload, the original address of entry 2 contains the replacement tag code.

Actual:

- The old extension units remain readable after CQ truncation.
- Replacement extension units are appended after the orphaned units.
- Recovery retains the orphaned units because the newly appended CQ entries now reference later extension addresses.

The controlled regression test is named:

```text
ConsumeQueueTest#testTruncateDirtyLogicFilesTruncatesConsumeQueueExtAndSurvivesReload
```

It uses no sleeps, randomized scheduling, or external services. On the latest unmodified `develop` baseline under JDK 8, it failed at the same business assertion in 5/5 isolated Maven/JUnit processes: expected replacement tag code `202`, but the original orphan still returned `102`.

## Impact

After CommitLog/CQ rollback followed by rebuilding, unreachable ConsumeQueueExt units remain between retained and replacement units. This leaks persistent store space and cannot be repaired by a later restart, because recovery truncates only after the newest referenced extension address.

## Suggested fix

- Route every normal scan exit through the CQExt truncation tail instead of returning early.
- Continue deleting wholly dirty tail CQ files until the last retained entry is found.
- Treat an empty first slot as an empty tail file and continue scanning the preceding retained file.
- If a retained CQ entry references CQExt, truncate after its last retained extension address; if no retained CQ entry references CQExt, physically clear the extension files so stale bytes cannot reappear during reload/recovery.
- Make the full-clear path recoverable when an extension mapped file is still referenced: retain failed mappings, block address reuse while cleanup is pending, and allow a later retry after the reader releases the buffer.
- When recovery finds no CQ file, clear any loaded CQExt files so a crash between CQ deletion and extension cleanup self-heals on restart.
- Preserve the non-destructive `deleteFile=false` overload by not physically truncating CQExt while detached CQ files remain on disk.
- Add partial-file, empty/full-tail-file, full-truncation, cleanup-failure/retry, replacement-write, and reload/recovery regression coverage.

## Related work checked

- #2570/#2572 only change when recovery invokes `truncateDirtyLogicFiles`; they do not truncate CQExt.
- #2571/#2573 discuss the physical-offset boundary condition, not extension cleanup.
- #10417/#10418 fixes stale minimum offsets after all CQ files are deleted; it does not reach or repair CQExt tail truncation.
- Open #9728/#9729 handles an empty last mapped file in `correctMinOffset`, a different method and postcondition.
- #6343 concerns deleting the CQExt directory when a topic is deleted.
- #10733 touches a different method in `ConsumeQueue` (`estimateMessageCount`) and does not change truncation.

Immediate pre-publication searches across open and closed issues and open, closed, and merged pull requests for `ConsumeQueueExt`, `truncateDirtyLogicFiles`, `truncateByMaxAddress`, extension truncation, and orphaned extension data found no equivalent report, claimed fix, or assignee.

Issue #2254: [syscall] Optimize dlfcn lookup cycle detection with graph coloring

## Summary

The visited set introduced in #2093 (PR #2253) uses a heap-allocated `BTreeSet<usize>` per lookup call. This works correctly but allocates on every `lookup()` invocation and has O(log n) per-node checks. A graph coloring scheme could eliminate the allocation and provide O(1) visited checks.

## Proposed Approach

Replace the per-lookup `BTreeSet` with an atomic generation counter stored directly in each dependency node:

1. **Add an atomic epoch field outside the mutex**, accessible without locking:
   ```rust
   struct DlNode {
       lib: Mutex<DynamicLibrary>,
       last_visited_epoch: AtomicU64,
   }
   ```

2. **A global atomic epoch counter** incremented at the start of each `lookup()` call.

3. **Check-and-stamp before locking** each dependency:
   ```rust
   let epoch = CURRENT_EPOCH.load(Relaxed);
   if dlnode.last_visited_epoch.swap(epoch, AcqRel) == epoch {
       continue; // already visited this epoch
   }
   ```

## Trade-offs

| Aspect | BTreeSet (current) | Graph coloring |
|---|---|---|
| Allocation | One BTreeSet per lookup | None |
| Per-node cost | O(log n) | O(1) atomic CAS |
| Concurrency | Naturally per-thread | Needs care with concurrent lookups sharing epochs |
| Structural change | None | Requires wrapping `Arc<Mutex<DynamicLibrary>>` in a new `Arc<DlNode>` type |

## Affected Files

- `src/libs/syscall/src/dlfcn/syscall/dynlib.rs` — dependency storage type and lookup logic
- `src/libs/syscall/src/dlfcn/syscall/dlopen.rs` — dependency construction and binding

## References

- #2093 — original bug (visited set fix)
- #2253 — PR implementing the BTreeSet approach

The corrected XGC reader in [Fides MR !236](https://gitlab.kitware.com/vtk/fides/-/merge_requests/236) exposed several related correctness issues in `ArrayHandleXGCCoordinates` and `CellSetExtrude`. Fides currently works around these issues so it can continue to build against the current Viskores release. The underlying behavior should be corrected in Viskores, followed by a cleanup in Fides once the fixed Viskores version is part of the supported dependency baseline.

A local prototype has confirmed the changes described below, but it has not been prepared as an upstream branch or pull request.

## Viskores issues

### 1. CellSetExtrude factories use the global plane count for partitions

The `make_CellSetExtrude` overloads that accept `ArrayHandleXGCCoordinates` construct the cell set with `coords.GetNumberOfPlanes()`. For a partitioned XGC data set this is the global plane count, not the number of coordinate planes stored in the partition.

They should use `coords.GetNumberOfPlanesOwned()` so that:

- `CellSetExtrude::GetNumberOfPlanes()` reports the local plane count.
- Point and cell counts match the coordinate array in the partition.
- Local cell IDs and logical plane indices stay within the partition.

This applies to the `ArrayHandle`, const-vector, and moved-vector factory overloads.

### 2. Optimized XGC coordinate fetches ignore PlaneStartId

`ArrayHandleXGCCoordinates` stores both the total number of planes and the partition `PlaneStartId`. Direct portal access and the optimized topology fetch paths do not consistently distinguish local logical plane indices from global plane indices. In particular, point-topology fetches can evaluate a partition as if its first local plane were global plane zero.

The optimized `CellSetExtrude` point and cell fetches must apply `PlaneStartId` exactly once. A possible implementation is an explicit local-plane portal method used by `FetchExtrude`, while retaining well-defined global access for existing portal calls.

Tests should compare optimized worklet fetches with portal coordinates for a partition whose `PlaneStartId` is nonzero.

### 3. ReverseConnectivityExtrude always wraps at extrusion endpoints

`ReverseConnectivityExtrude` currently has no periodicity state. It therefore treats the plane before plane zero as the final plane and reports cells across both endpoints even when `CellSetExtrude::GetIsPeriodic()` is false.

The cell-set periodic flag should be propagated into the execution connectivity. For a nonperiodic extrusion:

- Points on the first plane must not report incident cells from the final cell plane.
- Points on the final plane must not report incident cells from the first cell plane.
- Interior points must retain both adjacent cell-plane contributions.
- Periodic behavior must remain unchanged.

The existing reverse-connectivity constructor should remain source compatible if practical, with its current periodic behavior as the default.

### 4. ArrayHandleXGCCoordinates cannot represent fractional plane positions

XGC field-following values such as `dpot` are mapped to half planes. `ArrayHandleXGCCoordinates` currently represents only integer plane positions, which forces Fides to materialize a full basic coordinate array after rotating every point by half a plane.

Add an optional floating-point plane offset, defaulting to zero, and apply it when computing `phi` for both point and wedge coordinates:

```text
phi = (globalPlane + planeOffset) * deltaPhi
```

The offset must be preserved through:

- `ArrayHandleXGCCoordinates` metadata and portals.
- Constructors and `make_ArrayHandleXGCCoordinates` overloads, with defaults that preserve existing call sites.
- Serialization and deserialization, with compatibility considered for existing serialized data.
- Point and wedge coordinate fetches on supported devices.

## Viskores test coverage

Add focused coverage in `UnitTestArrayHandleXGCCoordinates` and `UnitTestCellSetExtrude` for:

- Total planes differing from locally owned planes.
- A nonzero `PlaneStartId`.
- A fractional plane offset such as `0.5`.
- Optimized cell and point topology worklets returning the same coordinates as portal access.
- Periodic reverse connectivity.
- Nonperiodic reverse connectivity at both endpoints and on an interior plane.
- Factory overloads constructing the correct local plane count.
- Serialization round-trip of all XGC coordinate metadata.

The execution-path tests should use the Viskores invoker and remain portable to the supported device adapters.

A maintainer on the project thefrederiksen/devthrottle (C#) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #2653: The Gateway test lock's 45-minute MaxWait equals a real run, so a queued run can never acquire

A second run of `CcDirector.Gateway.Tests` can **never** acquire the per-user test lock. `MaxWait` is **45 minutes**; a healthy full run measures **48.88 minutes**. The waiter's deadline expires before the holder can possibly finish, so it ends with **zero tests executed** after three quarters of an hour. This is arithmetic, not load or bad luck.

## The conclusion, settled over a day of hitting it

**Fix the lock. Do not add instruments around it.** Every mitigation tried has needed a caveat, and the caveats now outnumber the advice - because *the queue makes every instrument lie*:

| instrument | what it reports about a queued run | what is actually true |
|---|---|---|
| a human reading CPU counters | "wedged" - flat whole-second CPU | that is what polling looks like |
| the run's own exit | "broken build" - zero tests, no summary | it never started |
| `--blame-hang` | "hang" - and it kills the process | its inactivity timer counts lock waiting |

None of the three is wrong about what it measures. All three are measuring a process that has not started. No downstream tooling repairs that.

`--blame-hang` deserves its own line because it was proposed here as the fix and does not survive: to be safe while queued its timeout must exceed 45 minutes, but a healthy run is 48.88, so the safe setting and the useful setting do not overlap. It is safe **only once you already hold the lock**.

## What it cost on 2026-09-02

- A healthy 48.88-minute run was **diagnosed as wedged and killed eight minutes short**, on two signals that distinguish nothing: flat whole-second CPU, and no writes to `bin` since the build (true of every run).
- Two separate sessions waited and got **zero tests** - one 30 minutes, one the full 45.
- A run was killed by its own `--blame-hang` watchdog at 12 minutes while the lock log on the same process printed `THIS IS NOT A HANG`.
- All of this during a **live production incident**, where it was the single largest delay in verifying the fix.

## Scope - the boundary is the ASSEMBLY, not the filter

- Any run that **loads `CcDirector.Gateway.Tests`** takes the lock, filtered or not: `GatewayTestSuiteLock` is acquired by a `[ModuleInitializer]`, which fires on assembly load before any test and regardless of `--filter`.
- **Other assemblies are unaffected**, filtered or not. Observed: a full `Gateway.UnitTests` run (3,235 tests, 2m20s) completed normally while another worktree held the Gateway.Tests lock.

## Telling a queue from a real failure

**Zero tests executed = the queue.** **Nonzero test count with named failures = real failures, go read them.** It is a number the run reports about itself, not a judgement about who held what when. (An earlier version of this issue mis-attributed a real stale-database failure to the queue; that is retracted in the comments, and this discriminator is why it should not have happened.)

## Options, in order of value

1. **Make the suite hermetic so concurrent runs are safe, and delete the lock.** The lock exists because runs destroy each other - shared roots, ports, machine-wide singletons. Removes the serialisation instead of tuning it. Largest win, largest cost.
2. **Make the suite fast enough that the conflict cannot arise** - see #2655; 65% of test time is a handful of tests sleeping on fixed deadlines.
3. **Derive `MaxWait` from the measured suite duration** rather than pinning a literal, so the two cannot silently drift back into conflict as the suite grows.

## Working rules until it is fixed

- **Never queue.** Check the lock is free first - exclusive-open on the lock file, or scan for a `testhost.exe` under a `Gateway.Tests` path.
- **If it is held, use CI.** No lock, clean runner, cannot end in zero tests, blocks nobody. ~68 minutes for the whole .NET job against 49 local - about twenty minutes for the guarantee of getting an answer at all.
- **Read a zero-test timeout as the queue**, and do not go hunting a test that broke.

Issue #8: RFC: Decision authority, mission modes, evidence maturity, and stagnation escalation

## Summary

Explore a protocol-level extension for four orthogonal semantics that are currently implicit in Agent Relay:

1. **decision authority** — who is allowed to decide *what*;
2. **mission mode** — what kind of work a pass is actually performing;
3. **claim/evidence maturity** — how strongly a relied-upon claim is established;
4. **stagnation escalation** — when repeated failure should trigger a role/lens change instead of another same-role retry.

A fifth concept, **planning-context completeness**, is included as an exploratory/non-normative mechanism for deciding how much execution autonomy is safe without rating or profiling the human user.

This RFC is informed by Anthropic's June 16, 2026 research report, ["Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise"](https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-code-expertise), based on a privacy-preserving analysis of ~400,000 Claude Code sessions between October 2025 and April 2026.

The useful lesson is not that Agent Relay should score user expertise or optimize for longer autonomous action chains. The useful lesson is that effective agentic work separates **planning authority**, **execution autonomy**, and **verifiable success**.

Agent Relay already has the primitives needed to make those distinctions explicit: five stable roles, Reviewer lenses, mutation boundaries, immutable snapshots, evidence hierarchy, Verifier checkpoints, finding lifecycle, and Integrator readiness authority.

## Relationship to RFC #6

This RFC is deliberately separate from #6, **Runtime adapters and bounded iterative review loops**.

The intended boundary is:

> **RFC #6 governs control flow. This RFC governs decision semantics.**

RFC #6 asks:

- how repeated passes execute;
- how review cycles are bounded;
- how runtime state, cancellation, budgets, and termination work;
- how external runtimes/adapters may execute Agent Relay passes.

This RFC asks:

- who owns mission, architecture, implementation, verification interpretation, and readiness decisions;
- what category of work is occurring;
- how strong the evidence for a claim actually is;
- when repeated failure requires escalation or replanning.

A runtime or bounded review cycle defined by #6 MAY consume these semantics, but should not define them.

## Prior art / research signal

Anthropic's report describes several observations that map cleanly onto Agent Relay protocol concerns:

### Planning versus execution decisions

The report separates meaningful session decisions into:

- **planning** — what to do, which approach to take, what counts as done;
- **execution** — which files to change, what code to write, which commands to run.

In the observed sessions, users made about 70% of planning decisions while Claude made about 80% of execution decisions.

For Agent Relay, the important implication is:

> **Execution autonomy does not imply planning authority.**

An agent may be allowed to autonomously edit many files, run commands, or operate a deployment while remaining prohibited from changing the mission, architecture, acceptance criteria, or definition of done.

### Nine work modes

Anthropic classifies sessions into nine work modes:

- building;
- fixing;
- testing;
- orchestrating;
- operating software;
- understanding;
- planning;
- analyzing data;
- communicating / document work.

These should not become Agent Relay roles. They describe the **kind of work**, not the responsibility/authority model.

### Verified success

Anthropic distinguishes transcript-judged success from **verified success**. Their strict measure requires judged success plus at least one hard verifiable signal, such as matching Git activity, a passing test suite, or other strong evidence.

Agent Relay already says evidence beats assertions and has an evidence hierarchy. The opportunity is to make the **maturity of a specific relied-upon claim** explicit and portable across passes.

### Recovery from trouble

The report treats errors, failed tests, repeated attempts, and user pushback as failure/trouble signals. Sessions with greater task-specific expertise recover more often from trouble.

Agent Relay should not score or simulate human expertise. It can, however, encode the useful recovery behavior: repeated failed attempts or contradictory evidence should trigger a **protocol escalation**, not indefinite same-role retries.

### Task-specific expertise

Anthropic explicitly treats expertise as task-specific rather than occupational or general ability. Their classifier looks at framing precision, requested verification, and whether the user corrects the agent or vice versa.

Agent Relay should not adopt a `novice/intermediate/expert` user rating. The actionable substitute is to measure whether the **planning context required for safe autonomous execution is complete**.

## Design principle

**Separate responsibility, scrutiny, work type, decision authority, and evidence strength.**

The existing axes remain:

```text
Role
  = who is responsible for the pass

Reviewer lens
  = what a Reviewer scrutinizes
```

This RFC proposes additional orthogonal axes:

```text
Mission mode
  = what kind of work is being performed

Decision authority
  = which decisions this actor/pass may make

Evidence maturity
  = how strongly a relied-upon claim is established

Escalation state
  = whether continuing the same route is still justified
```

None of these should create a sixth role.

Add a protocol concept describing **which classes of decisions are delegated to which actor/role for the current mission**.

Example:

```text
Decision authority:
- Mission / desired outcome: User
- Architecture / acceptance criteria: User + Integrator
- Implementation mechanics: Builder
- Environment procedure: Executor
- Evidence interpretation: Verifier
- Readiness / reconciliation: Integrator
```

Issue #217: [P1][performance] Make follower retrieval and diff calculation linear, bounded, and rate-limit aware

## Background

Because every cursor is fetched sequentially without an upper bound and a bidirectional `Array.includes()` diff is then performed, API request count, CPU usage, and memory usage can all grow without bound for large channels.

## Current path

- [`lib/accessTwitch.ts`](https://github.com/NPJigaK/twitch-follower-checker/blob/37c0a40dc67d70110448d28ca7f6acae600b45ce/lib/accessTwitch.ts#L63-L83): recursively fetches pages with `first=100` until the cursor is exhausted
- [`lib/accessTwitch.ts`](https://github.com/NPJigaK/twitch-follower-checker/blob/37c0a40dc67d70110448d28ca7f6acae600b45ce/lib/accessTwitch.ts#L89-L100): runs `includes` in both directions inside `filter`

Worst-case comparison counts:

- 10,000 items: approximately 200 million
- 25,000 items: approximately 1.25 billion
- 50,000 items: approximately 5 billion (approximately 9.2 seconds in an isolated Node measurement for disjoint sets)
- 100,000 items: approximately 20 billion

50,000 followers require at least 500 API pages, and 100,000 followers require 1,000 pages. This can lead to HTTP 429 responses, long main-thread blocking, memory growth, and an unresponsive browser tab.

## Implementation direction

- Use `Set` / `Map` ID lookups and make the diff O(N)
- Replace recursive pagination with an explicit loop
- Maintain a visited-cursor set
- Add page, item, and elapsed-time budgets
- Support cancellation through `AbortController`
- Display progress
- Handle `Ratelimit-Remaining` / `Ratelimit-Reset`
- Deduplicate by `user_id`
- Treat `total` as a diagnostic value because it changes dynamically
- Debounce the quick filter and benchmark large `rowData`
- Define the maximum supported item count as a product requirement

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Diff calculation is O(N) with respect to the old/current item counts
- [ ] Benchmarks for 10k / 25k / 50k / 100k fixtures are retained in CI or as performance tests
- [ ] Duplicate cursors do not cause unbounded fetching
- [ ] Duplicate users do not appear more than once in the display or diff
- [ ] No repeated requests are sent before the reset time after a 429 response
- [ ] State and baseline are not updated after cancellation
- [ ] A snapshot that exceeds the page/time budget is treated as incomplete
- [ ] Main-thread long tasks and heap usage are compared before and after the fix using a Chrome trace

## Evidence

- [Twitch API: Get Channel Followers](https://dev.twitch.tv/docs/api/reference/#get-channel-followers)
- [Twitch API: Pagination and rate limits](https://dev.twitch.tv/docs/api/guide/)
- [ECMAScript: Array.prototype.includes](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/indexed-collections.html#sec-array.prototype.includes)

# QA & Security Test Suite — Request / Object-Level Authorization

## 1. Issue Summary & Test Strategy

### Summary

Request-Level Authorization and Object-Level Authorization are core security boundaries of the system.

This test suite MUST ensure that:

- no unauthorized request is executed;
- no unauthorized object is returned, updated, deleted, shared, or otherwise affected by side effects;
- authorized access is not incorrectly denied;
- `deny` precedence is always enforced correctly;
- default-deny behavior is always preserved;
- authorization cannot be bypassed through special Roles, special Users, internal APIs, caches, repositories, pagination, batch operations, or alternate execution paths;
- current behavior becomes a permanent regression contract so future DSL / Expression Engine / Role Hierarchy / ABAC / PBAC changes cannot silently alter existing semantics;
- malformed, adversarial, or unsupported authorization input MUST fail closed;
- authorization behavior is deterministic and independent of Statement load order, database row order, cache state, or evaluation order beyond explicitly defined semantics.

### Security Invariants

The following invariants MUST be treated as immutable and verified across Unit, Integration, and Regression suites:

- Request authorization:
  ```text
  deny if ANY matching deny evaluates true
  else allow if ANY matching allow evaluates true
  else deny
  ```

- Object authorization:
  ```text
  visible(object) =
      ANY(matching allow predicates)
      AND NOT ANY(matching deny predicates)
  ```

- No matching `allow` => deny.

- `deny` MUST override `allow`.

- Object authorization MUST happen database-side before pagination whenever queryable object authorization applies.

- Authorization MUST NOT fall back to in-memory filtering.

- The same effective Statement set MUST produce the same authorization decision regardless of Statement ordering.

- No built-in Role/User may bypass the common authorization pipeline.

- Invalid or unsupported authorization expressions MUST fail closed.

- API path regex MUST use RE2/J only.

- HTTP method matching is case-sensitive:
  - valid: `GET`, `POST`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, ...
  - wildcard: `*`
  - invalid examples: `get`, `Post`, `patch`

- `effect` is case-sensitive:
  - `allow`
  - `deny`

- `target.type` is case-sensitive:
  - `request`
  - `object`

- Multiple `conditions[]` entries use logical AND.

- OR / grouping / NOT are expressed inside conditions.

Issue #1690: SandboxDependencyManager caches installed requirements by sandbox name, not instance -- stale on container replacement

## Summary

`SandboxDependencyManager` (`src/xagent/core/tools/adapters/vibe/sandboxed_tool/sandboxed_tool_wrapper.py`) tracks installed pip requirements in a process-wide class-level dict keyed only by `sandbox.name`:

```python
_sandbox_installed_requirements: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
...
sandbox_key = sandbox.name
...
installed = cls._sandbox_installed_requirements.get(sandbox_key, set())
missing = sorted(required - installed)
if not missing:
    return
```

Sandbox lifecycle names are logical/stable (`SandboxManager.make_sandbox_name(lifecycle_type, lifecycle_id)`), not tied to a specific container instance. When a container is evicted (capacity pressure, idle reclamation) or rebuilt (mismatch reconcile) and a *new* container is created under the *same* logical name, `SandboxDependencyManager` still has the old container's "already installed" entry cached. `ensure_requirements()` then skips installation into the fresh container's filesystem, even though it has none of those packages.

## Impact

A tool (or MCP connector, e.g. anything routed through `list_tools_in_sandbox`/`_ensure_dependencies`) can then fail with an import error or missing binary the first time it runs against the replaced container -- `mcp` package absent for a freshly recreated sandbox is the concrete case that came up in review, but this affects every caller of `SandboxDependencyManager.ensure_requirements()`.

## Suggested direction

Key the installed-requirements (and lock) maps by something that changes across a container replacement -- sandbox instance identity/generation, or invalidate/evict the cache entry whenever `SandboxManager` deletes or replaces a sandbox for a given lifecycle name (there's already a `reconcile_delete`/eviction path in `sandbox_manager.py` that could call `SandboxDependencyManager`'s cache invalidation, or `resolve_primary_sandbox()`'s callers could pass something identity-bearing instead of relying on `.name` alone). Add a regression test using two distinct `Sandbox`-shaped objects that happen to share the same `.name`.

## Context

Surfaced during review of #1682. That PR didn't touch `SandboxDependencyManager`'s keying at all -- it only fixed what gets *passed in* as the `sandbox` argument (unwrapping a `SandboxLeaseProvider` first). This name-only caching predates that PR and already applied to every other sandboxed tool's dependency install (`_ensure_dependencies`). Filing separately rather than folding into that narrower bug fix.

Issue #1521: Emit HLSL helper declarations before their call sites

## Problem

Materialized helper definitions can be emitted after HLSL functions that call them. HLSL does not provide C-style implicit function declarations, so DXC reports the call as an undeclared identifier even when an exact definition appears later in the same artifact.

This is separate from helper materialization and overload binding: the concrete symbol and body both exist, but declaration order makes the artifact invalid.

## Expected behavior

Emit HLSL functions in dependency order or generate legal forward declarations for reachable helpers. Preserve overload identity, parameter direction, arrays, resources, and generated names exactly between declarations, definitions, and calls.

## Acceptance criteria

In a JS/TS file that contains at least one real function or class, code at **module top level** —
IIFEs, callbacks passed to top-level calls, bare driver calls, and initialiser calls — belongs to no
extracted unit. The call graph only scans emitted units' code, so calls made by that code, including
calls to sinks, do not become edges — as the executed run below shows.

A sink reachable through top-level bootstrap code alone therefore gets no incoming edge from it, as
the `x.js` run below shows. This is the false-negative direction.

## Reproduced at `b501962`, with a control

`x.js` — the sink is a defined function so edges to it are recordable, and the file has real functions

```javascript

function realFn() { sink(); }              // CONTROL
(function boot() { sink(); })();           // IIFE
[1].forEach(function () { sink(); });      // callback
main();                                    // bare driver call
function main() { return 2; }
const initv = sink();                      // initialiser
```

```
UNITS: ['x.js:sink', 'x.js:realFn', 'x.js:main']
CALL GRAPH:
    x.js:realFn -> ["x.js:sink"]
edges to sink: [["x.js:realFn",["x.js:sink"]]]
```

The control edge `realFn -> sink` is present, so edges to defined sinks are recordable and a null
result is not a broken harness. The IIFE, the callback, the bare `main()` and the initialiser contribute
nothing to the graph above — the only edge printed is the control's — and `boot` is absent from the

286|      ts.SyntaxKind.FunctionDeclaration,
287|      ts.SyntaxKind.FunctionExpression,
...
301|    return sourceFile
302|      .getDescendantsOfKind(ts.SyntaxKind.FunctionDeclaration)
303|      .filter((fn) => fn.getName() && isModuleLevel(fn));

Issue #64: ci: scheduled cleanup of unreferenced GHCR image versions (manifest-safe)

## Problem

GHCR packages for this repo accumulate image versions that are no longer referenced by any tag as `latest`/semver move to newer builds. Nothing prunes them, so they pile up in the GHCR UI.

Raw untagged counts today — **upper bound only**: these include *live* multi-arch child manifests (see constraint below), so they are **not** the deletable set:

| package | untagged versions (raw) |
|---|---|
| `base-notebook` / `base-notebook-ubi9` | 20 / 23 |
| `docker-stacks-foundation` / `-ubi9` | 20 / 23 |
| `minimal-notebook-ubi9` | 20 |
| most others | 2–4 |

This is **not** the `sha-<short>` tag problem fixed in `documentation` (#20/#21): `build.yml` has no `type=sha` rule and tags are already clean (`latest` + semver). Same UI symptom, different cause.

## Critical constraint: untagged ≠ deletable (reachability)

Deletion safety is about **reachability, not untaggedness**. Multi-arch images (`jamovi-ubi9`, `r-base-ubi9` build `linux/amd64` + `linux/arm64`) publish a tagged manifest **list** whose per-platform child manifests are themselves **untagged but live** (referenced by the index). Deleting an untagged version that is still referenced by a tagged index **irreversibly breaks pulls for that platform** (e.g. arm64) while amd64 still looks healthy.

A version is safe to delete **only if it is unreferenced by every tagged manifest list in the package** — proven by enumerating each tag → manifest list → child descriptors, not by reading the "untagged" flag.

## Proposed solution

A scheduled cleanup workflow (cron, alongside the existing `trivy-scheduled-rescan` / `base-drift` jobs) that deletes only **unreferenced** versions, with these guardrails:

- **Reachability-based selection** — exclude any digest reachable from any tag (including multi-arch child descriptors); never select on untaggedness alone.
- **Prove the tool before trusting it** — evaluate a candidate (`dataaxiom/ghcr-cleanup-action`, `snok/container-retention-policy@v3`, or equivalent) and **require its dry-run output on a multi-arch package to show the tagged index digest AND both platform child digests are retained**. Pin to a full commit SHA. A "manifest-aware" label is not sufficient evidence.
- **Race safety** — an explicit package allowlist generated from the build matrix; a minimum-age threshold for untagged deletion; a `concurrency` group (and/or schedule) so cleanup never overlaps `build`/publish runs (a just-built child can momentarily look unreferenced).
- **Least-privilege** — `permissions: packages: write` only.
- **Dry-run first** — ship in report-only mode; enable deletion only after the dry-run + cross-platform pull checks pass.

## Acceptance

- Cleanup deletes only versions unreferenced by any tag; tagged versions and live multi-arch child manifests are retained.
- Verified on a multi-arch package (`jamovi-ubi9` or `r-base-ubi9`): after a run, the tag still pulls on **both** `amd64` and `arm64`.
- Restricted to an explicit allowlist of this repo's packages, with a minimum-age threshold, and guaranteed not to run concurrently with `build`/publish.

## Summary
The HIER benchmark added in #344 runs on a **generated** dataset so it is reproducible from a clean checkout with no download and no licence gate. That covers the *shapes* — tree and multi-parent DAG, subtree sizes spanning four orders of magnitude — but it does not establish the constants on real data, and it has no cross-engine baseline at all. `benchmarks/hier/README.md` lists these under "Not yet covered"; this issue is that list, made actionable.

## 1. Real ontologies at scale
`examples/ontology_loader.rs` already reads the published formats — OBO, NCBI `nodes.dmp`, GeoNames `hierarchy.txt`, prefix-coded (ATC, MITRE ATT&CK), generic edge lists, generated calendar — and reports the probe verdict, encoding, space and build time. What is missing is running it on the full files and recording the numbers.

Targets, and what each is expected to show:

| Source | Size | Expected verdict |
|---|---|---|
| NCBI Taxonomy | ~1.3M nodes | tree → nested-set; the scale case for build time and 12 B/node |
| GeoNames hierarchy | ~330k | tree → nested-set |
| ATC | ~6.5k | strict 5-level tree; the clean prefix case |
| MONDO / HPO | ~25k / ~19k | mostly tree, some multi-parent |
| **Gene Ontology** | ~50k | **declines** — width approaches leaf count |
| MITRE ATT&CK + CWE | ~1k / ~1.4k | tree via prefix / edge list |

The Gene Ontology row is the one to publish loudest. A high-width DAG is where a 2-hop index is the right structure and OEH refuses to build, and reporting that on the real file is more credible than any speedup. Verified on a GO-shaped synthetic (width 500 > cap 179); the real file has not been run.

Licence note: everything above is open. UMLS/SNOMED stay behind `--i-have-a-licence` and no ontology data gets committed.

## 2. PLL / 2-hop baseline
The paper's claim is ~half the space and 6–7× faster build than 2-hop labelling *at query parity* on trees. Samyama has no PLL implementation, so this is **not reproduced** — `benchmarks/hier/README.md` says so. The reference repo `relationship-hierarchy-index` has a validated PLL in Python; porting it as a benchmark-only baseline (not engine code) would let us make or retract the claim on our own data.

This also matters for the decline path: above the width cap we tell users to go to a 2-hop index, and we should be able to show what that costs.

## 3. Cross-engine: Neo4j / TigerGraph
The corpus is Cypher and the dataset is generated, so porting the loader plus the H1–H8/H10 queries is mechanical. Home is `samyama-graph-competitor-benchmarks`. Worth doing precisely because the interesting classes are the ones where we are *not* obviously ahead (H1, H4, H6) — an external number tells us whether those are a Samyama planner problem or inherent to the shape.

## 4. TimescaleDB continuous aggregates for H10
The paper's head-to-head: the reference implementation matches TimescaleDB continuous aggregates to the unit (day 704,800; month 21,168,000) while also answering subsumption, which a continuous aggregate cannot. HIER class H10 is the same workload but has only been compared against Samyama's own expansion. Reproducing the TimescaleDB comparison in-engine would let us state the roll-up claim against the incumbent rather than against ourselves.

`benchmarks/hier/README.md` "Not yet covered" shrinks, with committed CSVs for whatever was run and an explicit note for anything that stays unrun and why.

Issue #371: OEH: near-trees fall into a gap — GeoNames is 98.7% a tree and is declined entirely

## Summary
The structural probe has two encodings and no middle. A poset that is a tree **except for a
handful of nodes** fails `is_tree()`, falls through to chain decomposition, and is then
declined because the chain width is unaffordable. Real administrative geography lands exactly
there.

Measured on GeoNames `hierarchy.txt` (ADM relations), 544,093 nodes:

| Parents per child | Children |
|---:|---:|
| 1 | 498,385 |
| 2 | 5,714 |
| 3 | 679 |
| 4 | 113 |
| 5 | 34 |

**6,540 of 504,925 children — 1.3% — have more than one parent.** That is enough to
disqualify the nested-set encoding for all 544,093 nodes:

```
index      : geo
encoding   : declined
chain width: 477763 (measured; over the cap)
DECLINED   : chain width 477763 exceeds cap 5901 (~8·sqrt(544093))
```

The probe is not making a mistake — chain decomposition genuinely costs O(n·width) and is
unaffordable at width 477k. The problem is that **there is no encoding between "perfect
tree" and "give up"**, so 98.7% of the structure is discarded because of 1.3% of it.

This matters more than a typical regime miss: geography is one of the three axes
[arXiv:2606.24677](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24677) unifies, and GeoNames is the paper's
own geography dataset. See `benchmarks/hier/results/real-ontologies.md` for the full run.

## Options

1. **Nested-set with an exception list.** Build the interval encoding over a spanning tree
   (each node's first parent), and keep the residual edges — 6,540 here — in a small
   side structure consulted only when the interval test says "no". Subsumption becomes
   `interval_contains(x, y) || exception_reachable(x, y)`. This is GRAIL's shape and it fits
   the 1.3% profile almost perfectly: the fast path answers ~99% of probes.
   The hard part is roll-up, which must not double-count a node reachable both through the
   tree and through an exception edge — the same set-semantics problem chain mode solves,
   now on a smaller set.
2. **Tree-cover / spanning-forest decomposition** — decompose into a few trees rather than
   many chains. Width becomes the number of trees, not the number of leaves.
3. **Report near-tree-ness in the decline.** Cheapest useful step regardless of which
   encoding lands: the diagnostic currently says only "width too high". It could say
   *"98.7% single-parent; 6,540 nodes carry the extra parents"*, which tells a user their
   data is one cleanup away from being indexable — quite different from "this poset is
   fundamentally unsuited".

Option 3 is worth doing on its own; option 1 is the substantive fix.

## Related
Part of #354. The decline path itself works correctly and is tested — see
`probe_declines_a_high_width_dag` — this is about the missing encoding, not a defect in the
existing one.

Issue #22: feat(analysis): Implement heuristic pedigree collapse (Ahnenschwund) predictor service

## Summary

Implement a new service within the MCP server that identifies missing nodes in the family graph (e.g., missing parent, missing sibling, missing spouse) where the probability of **pedigree collapse** (*Ahnenschwund*) is highest. 

Instead of searching for confirmed loops (which require complete graphs), this algorithm scans incomplete generational boundaries to prioritize high-yield research targets where endogamy or localized marriage patterns are most likely to merge ancestral branches.

---

## Service Architecture

### Recommended Class: `PedigreeCollapsePredictorService`

This service should sit alongside existing tree-traversal tools and expose methods for both batch scoring and targeted path evaluation.

#### Key Methods:
* `predict_collapse_candidates(tree_id: int, max_depth: int = 6, limit: int = 10)`
  Evaluates incomplete person nodes and ranks missing relation links by collapse probability.
* `calculate_node_collapse_score(person_id: str)`
  Internal heuristic scoring engine combining geographical, surname, temporal, and record-density factors.

---

## Heuristic Scoring Model & Algorithms

For each individual $P$ in the ancestral tree with incomplete relation links (missing mother, father, spouse, or siblings), compute a **Pedigree Collapse Probability Score ($S$)**:

$$S = S_{\text{location}} + S_{\text{surname}} + S_{\text{temporal}} + S_{\text{record\_density}}$$

### 1. Geographical Clustering ($S_{\text{location}}$)
* **Logic:** Marriages historically occurred within tight geographical perimeters. Missing events (birth, baptism, marriage, confirmation, death, residence) inherit locations from known events of the individual or their immediate ancestors/descendants via spatial propagation.
* **Scoring:**
  * High score if ancestors across distinct branches share the same or neighboring parishes/locations within a 10–15 km radius.
  * **Handling Missing Places:** Fall back to the nearest known location in the immediate sub-graph (e.g., if a birth place is missing, inherit the baptism place or parents' residence place). If no location is available across $N$ generations, set $S_{\text{location}} = 0$ (high uncertainty).

### 2. Surname Clustering ($S_{\text{surname}}$)
* **Logic:** Frequency of the same or phonetically similar surnames (or patronyms) across independent ancestral lines increases the likelihood of a shared ancestor.
* **Scoring:**
  * High score if the missing person's lineage contains surnames that already appear in other distinct branches of the tree.
  * **Married Surnames:** Include birth surnames, alternate names, and married surnames of female ancestors where patronymic naming or regional naming customs apply.

### 3. Recency Weighting ($S_{\text{temporal}}$)
* **Logic:** Recent missing links (18th–20th century) are significantly easier to research due to better record availability (civil registries, intact parish books) compared to older records (16th–17th century).
* **Scoring:**
  * Apply a mild, monotonic decay weight based on event dates:
    * Events $\ge$ 1850: Highest weight bonus (+0.25)
    * Events 1750–1849: Moderate weight bonus (+0.15)
    * Events < 1750: Low/No bonus (+0.0)

### 4. Record Density & Data Availability ($S_{\text{record\_density}}$)
* **Logic:** Nodes with high record density (e.g., known occupation, precise birth/baptism dates, multiple source citations) provide tighter constraints for matching potential candidates.
* **Scoring:** Reward missing links where surrounding nodes have detailed metadata; penalize links surrounded by empty "ghost" nodes.

---

## Input & Output Alignment Requirement

To ensure compatibility with LLM consumers (like Qwen or Gemini) and front-end UIs:
1. Every tool response **MUST** contain aligned human-readable text (`text` field) and structured data (`structuredContent` field).
2. The structured payload must include an `_ai_context` object providing explicit instructions to the AI on next steps.

---

A maintainer on the project openvibely/openvibely (Go) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #937: Failed plugin installs leave stale cache entries and block recovery

## Summary
A plugin install that fails partway can leave behind a directory that OpenVibely later treats as a completed installation. For example, after a marketplace download fails, reopening the Agent dialog shows the plugin under Installed, and clicking Install again skips the download even though the plugin has no skills or MCP files to run. This makes a transient install failure look successful and prevents users from recovering through the normal retry flow.

## Inspected component
The Agent plugin install/state workflow, including the local cache materialization path, plugin state discovery, the `POST /agents/plugins/install` handler, runtime bundle resolution, and the Agents modal catalog.

## Evidence and concrete failure paths
- `internal/agentplugins/plugins.go:1048-1095` `installPluginLocally` creates `cache/<marketplace>/<plugin>` at line 1069, then creates a `.tmp-<timestamp>` staging directory. If `materializePluginSource` fails at line 1081, cleanup removes only the staging directory at line 1082 and returns the error; the empty plugin parent remains.
- `internal/agentplugins/plugins.go:639-675` `newestVersionedDir` treats every child directory as a candidate without checking that it is a finalized version. If the cache parent is empty, it returns the parent itself at lines 663-665. If a process is interrupted before cleanup, the `.tmp-*` directory is also accepted as the newest candidate.
- `internal/agentplugins/plugins.go:827-895` `augmentInstalledFromLocalCacheAtRoot` enumerates any marketplace/plugin directory under `cache`, calls `newestVersionedDir`, and appends an `InstalledPlugin` with `Enabled: true` whenever a path is returned. It does not verify that the selected path contains a materialized plugin.
- `internal/agentplugins/plugins.go:193-205` `DiscoverState` includes this cache-derived entry in the state returned to the handler. The state therefore reports an installation that never completed, or points at an incomplete staging tree.
- `internal/handler/agent_handler.go:582-627` `installPluginForModalAgent` first discovers state and sets `alreadyInstalled` through `isPluginInstalled` at lines 589-592. On the next install request, the stale entry causes it to skip `installPluginFn` at lines 593-600, then continue to MCP startup and agent binding as though installation succeeded.
- `web/templates/pages/agents.templ:868-900` treats every state entry in `installed` as an installed catalog item, and `web/templates/pages/agents.templ:1238-1298` sends the current agent ID and shows the successful response as installed/enabled. The user can therefore see the plugin under `INSTALLED` and cannot repair it with the normal Install action.
- `internal/agentplugins/plugins.go:405-487` `ResolveRuntimeBundle` resolves the empty parent or staging directory, loads no skills or MCP servers, still appends an accumulator for that path, and can return a successful bundle with the plugin ID but no plugin resources. `EnsurePluginMCPRunning` also returns nil when that path produces no MCP servers at lines 536-549, so the absence may not produce a visible runtime error.

A concrete reachable sequence is:
1. A user opens an Agent plugin catalog and clicks Install for a marketplace plugin whose remote clone or local copy fails, such as a network interruption or invalid source.
2. The endpoint returns a controlled install error, but `installPluginLocally` leaves the empty cache parent behind.
3. The modal refreshes `/agents/plugins/state`; discovery reports the plugin as installed with the empty parent as its install path.
4. The user clicks Install again. `installPluginForModalAgent` sees the stale installed row, skips the materialization retry, and returns HTTP 200. If an agent is being edited, the handler can also persist the plugin ID onto that agent.
5. A later agent run sees the stale path and silently receives no plugin skills or MCP servers. An interrupted process can produce the same result with a leftover `.tmp-*` directory, even if the directory contains only partial files.

## Expected versus actual behavior
Expected: only a completed, usable plugin installation should appear in `PluginState.Installed`. A failed or interrupted materialization should leave no installed marker, should not be selected or enabled for an agent, and should allow the next Install request to retry. A valid prior version should remain usable if a later update fails.

Actual: the cache parent itself, or any staging child directory, is considered an installed version. The next install request skips materialization, the UI reports the plugin as installed, and runtime resolution can succeed with an empty resource bundle instead of reporting that the plugin is unavailable.

## Risk
A transient network, copy, or process failure can permanently strand a plugin in a false-installed state until the user manually deletes files under the application plugin root. Agents may persist a plugin that contributes no intended skills or tools, and runtime health can appear neutral because no MCP server is started to report a failure.

## Suggested implementation direction
Make cache discovery recognize only finalized installation directories and ignore `.tmp-*` or other staging names. An empty cache parent should return no install path rather than the parent itself. On materialization failure, remove the empty install root when it has no prior finalized version; preserve any existing valid version if the operation is an update. Keep the retry behavior driven by actual usable state, and consider returning a controlled resolution error when a selected plugin has no valid materialized resources instead of returning an empty successful bundle.

## Acceptance criteria
- A failed `materializePluginSource` call does not cause the plugin to appear in `DiscoverState().Installed`.
- A cache containing only an empty plugin parent or only `.tmp-*` directories is not reported as installed and does not block a subsequent install retry

https://ift.tt/12pRuNw



Introduction

Most users at one time or another have dealt with hierarchical data in a SQL database and no doubt learned that the management of hierarchical data is not what a relational database is intended for. The tables of a relational database are not hierarchical (like XML), but are simply a flat list. Hierarchical data has a parent-child relationship that is not naturally represented in a relational database table.

For our purposes, hierarchical data is a collection of data where each item has a single parent and zero or more children (with the exception of the root item, which has no parent). Hierarchical data can be found in a variety of database applications, including forum and mailing list threads, business organization charts, content management categories, and product categories. For our purposes we will use the following product category hierarchy from an fictional electronics store:

These categories form a hierarchy in much the same way as the other examples cited above. In this article we will examine two models for dealing with hierarchical data in MySQL, starting with the traditional adjacency list model.

The Adjacency List Model

Typically the example categories shown above will be stored in a table like the following (I’m including full CREATE and INSERT statements so you can follow along):

CREATE TABLE category(
        category_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
        name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
        parent INT DEFAULT NULL
);

INSERT INTO category VALUES(1,'ELECTRONICS',NULL),(2,'TELEVISIONS',1),(3,'TUBE',2),
        (4,'LCD',2),(5,'PLASMA',2),(6,'PORTABLE ELECTRONICS',1),(7,'MP3 PLAYERS',6),(8,'FLASH',7),
        (9,'CD PLAYERS',6),(10,'2 WAY RADIOS',6);

SELECT * FROM category ORDER BY category_id;
+-------------+----------------------+--------+
| category_id | name                 | parent |
+-------------+----------------------+--------+
|           1 | ELECTRONICS          |   NULL |
|           2 | TELEVISIONS          |      1 |
|           3 | TUBE                 |      2 |
|           4 | LCD                  |      2 |
|           5 | PLASMA               |      2 |
|           6 | PORTABLE ELECTRONICS |      1 |
|           7 | MP3 PLAYERS          |      6 |
|           8 | FLASH                |      7 |
|           9 | CD PLAYERS           |      6 |
|          10 | 2 WAY RADIOS         |      6 |
+-------------+----------------------+--------+
10 rows in set (0.00 sec)

In the adjacency list model, each item in the table contains a pointer to its parent. The topmost element, in this case electronics, has a NULL value for its parent. The adjacency list model has the advantage of being quite simple, it is easy to see thatFLASH is a child ofmp3 players, which is a child of portable electronics, which is a child of electronics. While the adjacency list model can be dealt with fairly easily in client-side code, working with the model can be more problematic in pure SQL.

Retrieving a Full Tree

The first common task when dealing with hierarchical data is the display of the entire tree, usually with some form of indentation. The most common way of doing this is in pure SQL is through the use of a self-join:

SELECT t1.name AS lev1, t2.name as lev2, t3.name as lev3, t4.name as lev4
FROM category AS t1
LEFT JOIN category AS t2 ON t2.parent = t1.category_id
LEFT JOIN category AS t3 ON t3.parent = t2.category_id
LEFT JOIN category AS t4 ON t4.parent = t3.category_id
WHERE t1.name = 'ELECTRONICS';

+-------------+----------------------+--------------+-------+
| lev1        | lev2                 | lev3         | lev4  |
+---------

Issue #1978: Browser persistent worker loses large-value chunks during sync

🤖 Browser clients using the persistent-worker topology cannot sync a streamed or otherwise oversized large value through the worker relay, even while fully online.

## Reproduction

The MusicAgent topology receipt in draft PR #1838 writes a multi-chunk Text value from a browser tab connected through the persistent SharedWorker relay. The reader never receives all rows. The sender transport later terminates with:

```text
Storage: chunk is unavailable
```

Removing every injected edge failure and reconnect leaves the failure deterministic. Replacing `insertStreaming` with an ordinary oversized Text write also fails, so this is not limited to the streaming API. Once the transport reaches this state, even a subsequent ordinary control write is blocked. A private `flushLocal()` barrier does not help.

## Isolation

- A local-only browser streaming receipt passes and therefore does not cover this topology.
- A Rust tab-like non-durable/deferred client → deferred relay → core receipt passes with a real streamed value.

Issue #69: v0.3.0: Durable Commit and explicit fsync/recovery guarantees

## Problem and goal
LayerFS currently acknowledges live-process visibility without guaranteeing that an acknowledged snapshot survives an OS crash or power loss. v0.3.0 should introduce an explicit, tested durability contract, starting with **durable public Commit**: after Commit returns successfully, the published snapshot, its dependencies, and the corresponding history/head changes survive the supported crash and recovery scenarios.

Related: #52 (v0.3.0 cloud native integration and S3-compatible persistence). This issue owns the local durability foundation and its acknowledgement contract; coordinate remote replication semantics with #52.

## Current behavior
- The Store configures SQLite `journal_mode=MEMORY`, `synchronous=OFF`, and `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, and rejects WAL Stores during opening.
- Workspace `fsync` currently validates spool state and completes capture; it does not provide a disk persistence guarantee. Spool segment files are unlinked after opening, so adding `sync_all()` alone would not make live edits recoverable.
- A public Commit can include multiple object-admission transactions, a staged-root transaction, and final publication. Durability cannot be estimated or implemented as one unconditional fsync per public operation.

Relevant code: `crates/layerfs-layerstack-store/src/schema.rs`, `objects.rs`, `workspace.rs`, `staging.rs`; `crates/layerfs-workspace/src/file_io.rs` and `lifecycle.rs`.

## Scope and acceptance
- [ ] Define acknowledgement guarantees for ordinary writes, application file/directory fsync, public Commit, initialization/Add, and remote replication. State which data and metadata each boundary protects, and distinguish process loss, OS crash/power loss, and loss of the storage device or host.
- [ ] Implement durable public Commit first. Persist all referenced canonical objects and required metadata before acknowledging the atomically published result; preserve conditional head updates, retained history, and v0.2 reconciliation semantics.
- [ ] Select the smallest recoverable SQLite journal/synchronization configuration. Evaluate WAL + FULL and an appropriate disk-backed rollback-journal alternative; do not merely change `synchronous` while leaving MEMORY journaling in place. Specify platform flush semantics, checkpointing, locking, Store creation/directory persistence, and migration/reopen compatibility.
- [ ] Handle I/O and synchronization failures without reporting false durable success. Define recovery and retry behavior when publication succeeds but its response is lost, and when the persistence outcome is uncertain.
- [ ] Make an explicit, separate decision on durable live-workspace file/directory fsync. If included, persist the recoverable edit representation and required metadata as well as bytes. If deferred, document the weaker uncommitted-workspace contract clearly; durable Commit must not imply that every successful application fsync is power-loss durable.
- [ ] Keep memory, dirty state, journal/WAL growth, and retry work bounded. Preserve canonical identities and protect published dependencies during recovery and cleanup.

## Correctness proof
- [ ] Exercise failures before/after object admission, staging, publication, synchronization, and acknowledgement; cover synchronization errors and lost replies.
- [ ] Reopen after failure and verify database integrity, acknowledged roots, history/heads, canonical IDs, and file bytes. Never expose a published root with missing dependencies or silently lose an acknowledged durable snapshot.
- [ ] Prove migration and supported reopen behavior for existing Stores, including recovery with required journal/WAL sidecars.
- [ ] Distinguish process-kill tests from evidence for OS-crash/power-loss behavior. Freeze the supported platform/storage assumptions and retain reproducible failure evidence.

## Performance validation
Measure the existing benchmark workloads under separately named profiles: current visibility-only baseline, durable Store publication, and durable Store plus live-workspace fsync if implemented. Preserve operation counts, fixtures, public calls, and timing boundaries.

Prioritize:
- SDK edit families, including canonical-count and capped length-changing cases: short edit + Commit latency.
- `payload_create_read`, `init_namespace`, `store_footprint`, `dedup_cross_file`, and `dedup_cdc_locality`: admission transaction count, dirty bytes, and journal/write amplification.
- `dedup_workspace_reuse`, `mixed_load_bearing`, and `git_tool_workflow`: sequential application synchronization.
- `dedup_branch_history`, especially unrelated history: 200 file fsync calls per step, or 100,000 at tier 500, plus directory syncs and repeated Commit.
- Tiny-file churn, namespace/directory operations, workspace locality, read-only execution, and clean Commit: retain batching and identify unnecessary persistence work.

- [ ] Report actual physical flush count/time, SQLite transaction count, Exec/admission/publication latency, p50/p95/p99, throughput, CPU/RSS, and storage growth. Keep preparation and recovery verification outside their unrelated performance timers.
- [ ] Account for journal/WAL sidecars in storage metrics and adapt the current closed-Store preparation/clone compatibility checks; do not reuse incompatible prepared Stores or omit durability files.
- [ ] Run paired measurements on the supported host-store topology, then regress affected family members and reliability proofs. Do not remove workload fsync calls or weaken the promised acknowledgement boundary to pass a target.

Issue #4883: Silent `process_kprobe` attribution loss when `checkprocfs.Check()` fails (Docker Desktop LinuxKit kind on Apple Silicon)

# What happened? How can we reproduce this?

When Tetragon v1.6.1 starts up on a Docker Desktop LinuxKit
`kind` cluster (a very common local-dev configuration on Apple
Silicon Macs), it emits a single **warning** about a procfs
inode mismatch and then continues running normally.
Downstream, **every** `process_kprobe` event originating from
any user-deployed pod reaches the exporter stream with empty
`binary`, `exec_id`, `flags`, and `pod` fields — effectively
classifying every attacker (or application) action as
"exec-only" and silently neutralising any pod-scoped
TracingPolicy. The failure mode is completely silent from the
operator perspective: Tetragon reports no error, processes events
at line rate, and looks healthy in every health probe.

An existing issue (#2257) documents the inode-mismatch warning
for the case where Tetragon fatally aborts at startup due to a
*different* follow-on problem (missing kernel features on that
particular environment). The scenario described here is more
dangerous precisely because Tetragon **does not** fail loudly
— security posture appears intact while attribution is
systematically broken.

## Source-level chain that explains the observation

The silent failure is a cascade across four pieces of Tetragon
source that together maintain the `execve_map` invariant:

1. `pkg/checkprocfs/checkprocfs.go:30-36` — compares
   `$procfs/1/ns/pid` inode against the hard-coded host
   PID-namespace init inode `0xEFFFFFFC` (= 4026531836) and
   emits the `"inode mismatch: procfs does not appear to be host
   procfs"` warning on mismatch. **The warning is non-fatal**:
   Tetragon continues booting.

2. `pkg/sensors/exec/procevents/proc_reader_linux.go:98-140, 396`
   — walks `$procfs` and seeds `execve_map`. On the affected
   environment, many entries are filtered out by the
   per-process namespace-read and pid-ns checks, producing a
   partial snapshot reported by the informational log line
   `"Read ProcFS %s appended %d/%d entries"`. In our
   reproduction on fresh Docker Desktop kind, we observe
   **39/95 (41%) filled**; on a GKE COS node with the same
   Helm release the same log says **486/486 (100%)**.

3. `bpf/process/bpf_fork.c:41-43` — the
   `kprobe/wake_up_new_task` handler enforces a hereditary
   invariant: a new task is added to `execve_map` **only if its
   parent is already in the map**:

   ```c
   parent = __event_find_parent(task);
   if (!parent)
       return 0;   /* new task NOT added */
   curr = execve_map_get(tgid);
   ```

   When the startup snapshot drops an ancestor, every
   descendant is permanently excluded from `execve_map`, even
   though the kprobe itself attaches correctly and fires for
   each `fork`.

4. `bpf/lib/bpf_task.h:147-168` (`event_find_curr`) +
   `bpf/process/bpf_process_event.h:342-359`
   (`event_find_curr_probe`) — at `process_kprobe` time, the
   4-step `real_parent` walk misses `execve_map` and falls back
   to `event_find_curr_probe`, which synthesises a minimal value
   from `BPF_CORE_READ(task, tgid)` but **does not** populate
   `binary`, `exec_id`, `flags`, or the pod object. The event
   is emitted with `MSG_COMMON_FLAG_PROCESS_NOT_FOUND`, reaches
   userspace, and is enriched against a process cache that has
   no entry for that PID — producing the empty JSON payload we
   observe.

Issue #5: feat(dryrun): visualize recursive calls and stack frames

## Problem

AlgoLang dry runs can reconstruct call trees and variable states, but recursive algorithms are still difficult for learners to follow. The current tabular output does not clearly show:

- when a recursive call creates a stack frame;
- which arguments and local variables belong to each invocation;
- the current recursion depth;
- which invocation is active;
- how return values propagate to callers; and
- when stack frames are created and removed.

This makes algorithms such as factorial, Fibonacci, recursive binary search, merge sort, and depth-first search harder to understand.

## Proposed enhancement

Add a recursion-focused dry-run visualization that displays the call hierarchy and active call stack alongside the existing variable timeline.

Example:

```text
Call tree
factorial(4)
└─ factorial(3)
   └─ factorial(2)
      └─ factorial(1) → 1
      ← 2
   ← 6
← 24

Active stack
┌───────┬──────────────┬───────────┬────────┐
│ Depth │ Call         │ Arguments │ Locals │
├───────┼──────────────┼───────────┼────────┤
│ 0     │ factorial(4) │ n = 4     │        │
│ 1     │ factorial(3) │ n = 3     │        │
│ 2     │ factorial(2) │ n = 2     │        │
└───────┴──────────────┴───────────┴────────┘
```

The visualization should use structured tracing data instead of parsing formatted terminal output.

## Suggested scope

- Represent each function invocation with its call ID, parent call ID, depth, arguments, local variables, status, and return value.
- Show frame creation, active execution, return, and removal.
- Highlight the active invocation at each replay step.
- Keep local variables separate for repeated calls to the same function.
- Support forward, backward, and random-access replay.
- Preserve the existing dry-run table for non-recursive programs.
- Keep deeply recursive output readable through depth limits or collapsed frames.
- Add at least one educational recursive `.algo` example.
- Expose the call-stack state through the Python API for future VS Code and graphical views.

## Possible CLI usage

```sh
algo dryrun examples/factorial.algo --calls
```

or:

```sh

Issue #1297: bug: Memory commit accepts malformed revisions and search can return text that entries() rejects

### Describe the bug

RFC 0014 and the Memory protocol name the backend as the final trust boundary: `commit()` must validate and atomically persist one complete Revision in the same transaction, and search must filter every candidate through the authoritative head manifest. The current implementation does not honor that contract.

This is not a default HTTP/MCP remember, revise, retire, or flush incident. Those paths go through `MemoryService`, which currently fills predecessor, hash, and projections itself. The gap is the public SPI: `MemoryCommit`, `MemoryWritePlan`, and `MemoryBackend` allow a writer to bypass the service and call `backend.commit()` directly. Tests and a later writer can already take that seam.

**What the contract says, and what the code does**

1. The protocol requires `MemoryUnitOfWork.commit()` to validate and atomically commit one complete Revision. `_validate_commit()` only checks family, the whole-document `content_hash`, revision +1, base identity, and equality of the active/projection version-id sets.
2. The RFC sequence diagram requires the backend to validate identity, predecessor, manifest, hash, and vectors. The implementation does not recompute the entry body hash, validate the direct predecessor, or require projections to match the authoritative entry.
3. The RFC schema draws a self-referencing foreign key on `previous_version_id`. `pc_memory_entry_versions.previous_version_id` is a plain string column.
4. The RFC requires search to revalidate active membership, exact version, and canonical bytes against the authoritative manifest. The implementation only confirms that the target is still the current head, so the index can act as a second content authority.
5. The RFC describes projections and indexes as rebuildable, non-authoritative copies. Hit text can come from an unrevalidated index/body and no longer line up with the manifest hash.

**What has already been reproduced**

1. A revision-1 entry with `previous_version_id="does-not-exist"` commits and reads back.
2. A body replaced with `tampered searchable body.` while keeping the hash of `User prefers black tea.` also commits.
3. In that corrupted state, `search()` returns the tampered body, while `entries()` raises `InvalidMemoryCitationError` for the same revision.
4. `entries()` also omits the `version.entry_content_hash` comparison that `_validate_anchor()` already performs.

Closing only the write path or only the read path leaves the loop open. Both sides should be fixed in one PR.

**What this gap can cause later**

Official product paths almost never construct a bad envelope today, so normal use usually does not show the damage. If the seam is taken, or if the service or a second writer later emits a bad commit, the likely consequences are:

1. Illegal history becomes durable authority. A hash is then a label written with the envelope, not a commitment.
2. A fake predecessor has almost no current read consumer, but later lineage, offline validation, or citation code that walks `previous_version_id` will not be able to rebuild history reliably.
3. After a body / declared / manifest hash mismatch, remember, revise, forget, and organize fail with `hash-mismatch`. The Memory can still be recalled but can no longer be governed.
4. If a projection or `searchable_text` diverges from the canonical row, search and automatic `POST /v1/context/prepare` injection can hand a different body to the model.
5. Context Pack and Handoff can consume text the authoritative manifest never committed.
6. A new adapter, migration script, or homemade `MemoryWritePlan` will copy the current thin checks as the contract, and the gap will spread.
7. Fixing only one side still lets dirty data in, or still lets search return it after it is in.

1. Use a PowerContext checkout with its dependencies installed.
2. Save the following as `repro_memory_integrity.py`.
3. Run:

```bash
python repro_memory_integrity.py
```
